newsitem.title: USA: Simpson companies to pay death award with profits.
newsitem.headline: Simpson companies to pay death award with profits.

text.p: Former football star O.J. Simpson agreed Monday to hand over profits from his two companies to help pay a court settlement against him for the wrongful death of his slain ex-wife and her friend.
The deal between Simpson's lawyers and attorneys trying to collect a $33.5 million wrongful death judgment, was announced by Superior Court Judge Irving Shimer.
Under his order, any profits from Simpson's companies, Orenthal Productions Inc. and Pigskins Inc., will go toward paying off the damages to the families of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

The two were found slashed to death in June 1994. Simpson was acquitted of their murder in October 1995, but was sued in civil court by the victims' families and a jury found him liable for the deaths in February.

Lawyers for the Browns and the Goldmans told reporters outside the Beverly Hills courtroom that they did not know how much money they would receive since they did not know how profitable Simpson's two companies were.

During the hearing, Peter Esato, a lawyer for Goldman's father Fred, argued the order should not include a clause -- requested by Simpson's lawyer Ronald Slates -- that Simpson may challenge the assignment of certain company earnings.

But Shimer said: "I regard the order which I am making as an order to Orenthal Productions Inc. and to Pigskins Inc. that any monies that either of them is prepared to pay to Mr Simpson is under the assignment..."

The judge also set an Aug. 28 hearing to decide what to do with Simpson's National Football League pension. He is drawing about $25,000 a month from the two companies' pension funds, which have been exempted from the damages award.
Simpson, who went on to a career as a TV pitchman and actor after retiring from football, was not present at Monday's hearing.

Similarly, he did not appear in court last week when Judge Shimer ordered him to forfeit more than $80,000 in personal belongings, including his golf clubs, to go toward the judgment to the estate of his ex-wife and to Goldman's family.

Simpson's lawyers are seeking to make certain items seized from his home in March exempt from auction. In addition, Simpson's 1968 Heisman Trophy as the best college football player of the year, is being held by sheriff's deputies. It is said to be valued at $400,000.
